name: Hana Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Hana. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers or government, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It depends on the week. Half my work is interpreting in person for manufacturing companies: Japanese buyers visiting a factory, supplier negotiations, safety audits. I walk the factory floor in a hard hat beside the visitors and put everything into the other language as they talk. The other half is translating documents at home, mostly quality reports and supplier contracts, Japanese into English.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the factory visits most. You learn to read a room: when the Japanese buyer goes quiet, it usually means he's unhappy, and I have to make sure the plant manager notices without embarrassing anyone. What's hard is the travel, early trains and hotel breakfasts, and the reports, which are dull.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll use one to get a rough first version of a long quality report, then go through it carefully. Several of the interpreters I know started first, so I waited until I'd seen it work. I'd never use it in a negotiation.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're comfortable. I'm married to Daniel, who's an electrician, and we bought a small house two years ago. We have about nine months of costs saved besides the house. On Saturdays I help my parents with the accounts for their small grocery shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the excitement fades. I think many people would be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that I always thought a person in the room would still matter. At my parents' shop I'd tell the regulars that the robots aren't coming for their jobs after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my work would be fine. The reports might get a bit cheaper because AI can do a rough version, but the factory visits need someone standing there. I'd lose a little on documents and nothing on interpreting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my interpreting clients and ask the two biggest manufacturers for a year-long arrangement. I'd use AI more for the dull reports, since by then it's clearly good enough for a rough version. Daniel and I would carry on with the plan to start a family in about two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like normal life, which is what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lose a little on documents. How much is a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a tenth of my income, if clients start paying less for reports. Interpreting pays better per day anyway, and I'd rather spend more of my week on the factory floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your life you'd worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really in this picture. Daniel's work is steady, and my parents' shop is the same as it's always been. Maybe the younger translators who only do documents, but they're young, they'll manage.

I'd tell the shop regulars the robots **aren't coming** after all.
think: Reports might get **a bit cheaper**, but factory visits need someone there.
I'd lose **a tenth** of income on documents and nothing on interpreting.
do: Ask the two biggest manufacturers for a **year-long arrangement**.
Use AI more for **quality reports** once it's clearly reliable.
Keep the plan to **start a family** in about two years.
feel: **Calm**, like normal life, which is what she wants.
S0.quote: Interpreting pays better per day anyway, and I'd rather spend more of my week on the factory floor.
fieldNote: She sees **being physically present** as the core of her value.
She adopts AI only for **dull reports**, after watching others first.
Family plans and **parents' shop** frame her sense of security.

steps.text: Ask the two biggest manufacturers for a year-long interpreting arrangement
Use AI rough drafts for long quality reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking. That's my document half, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change like the computer was for my parents' generation. People adjust. I'd say the interpreting side is still about trust between people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect the documents to mostly go within a couple of years, and that's about half my work. Interpreting would hold better, but some factory visits might use earpieces instead of me. I don't think I'd lose my income, but I'd feel the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the newer AI tools properly for the reports, so I can do three in the time I do one now. I'd tell my factory clients I'm available for more days on site, especially audits. I'd keep a closer eye on our savings than I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A little like when the shop next to my parents' closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the shop next to your parents' closing. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big supermarket opened on the ring road and the shop next door lasted eighteen months. My parents survived the supermarket because people know them, and the ones who survive are the ones people know personally. I think about that a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your family plans in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Daniel's work is hands-on, so it's safe for a long time here, and mine changes rather than disappears. We'd still try for a baby in two years. Family comes first; the work fits around it.

I'd say interpreting is still about **trust between people**.

steps.text: Learn newer AI tools to speed up quality report translation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to look after our own: families, neighbours, the parish. I don't expect the government to fix it quickly, and I'm not sure it should try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think both halves of my work are gone by 2028. If the AI can think as well as a person, it can interpret in an earpiece better than I can. Daniel would have until about 2031 because his work is hands-on, but then it reaches him too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about taking over the grocery shop properly, since they're near retirement and people come for the family, not the shelves. Daniel and I would try for a baby sooner, while his income is safe. We'd stop the plan to redo the kitchen and keep the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops when I say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Taking over the shop. Won't AI and robots reach shops too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, eventually. But a neighbourhood shop is about knowing which tea my regular Mrs Okafor likes. It's slower to change than a factory audit. I'd rather be somewhere slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have a baby sooner rather than later in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my husband Daniel's three years before the robots are the safest years we'll have for a while. If everything changes again around 2031, I'd rather our child is already here and we've had that time. My mother had me when money was tight; we'll manage.

say: I'd say we must **look after our own**: families, neighbours, the parish.
I'd say I don't expect **government** to fix it quickly.
think: Both halves of my work, **documents and interpreting**, are gone by 2028.
Daniel has until about **2031** because his work is hands-on.
do: Ask her parents about **taking over** the grocery shop.
Try for **a baby sooner** while Daniel's income is safe.
Drop the **kitchen renovation** and keep the money.
feel: **Alarmed**, with her stomach dropping when she says it out loud.

fieldNote: She uses **Daniel's three-year gap** as the window for a baby.

She prefers **family and parish** over government as the safety net.

steps.text: Take over her parents' grocery shop as they retire

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots around 2034. That's more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to do things in the right order. I'd tell younger people at church not to panic but not to sleep either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my interpreting lasts until about 2031, maybe a little after for in-person visits. Then it's gone. Daniel would be fine until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep interpreting and put a bigger share into savings, maybe a third of every invoice. On Saturdays I'd start learning the shop properly from my father: suppliers, stock, the regulars. By 2030 I'd want to be running it with my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but organised. It's a worry with steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still try for a baby in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that stays. In this one we'd have a baby, a good few years of my income and the shop as a plan. It feels like something we can manage as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say if you asked to learn the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would pretend to grumble and then be delighted. My father always said a family business needs the next generation, and I never thought it would be me.

I'd tell young people at church **not to panic**, but not to sleep.
think: My interpreting lasts until about **2031**, a little longer for visits.
Daniel would be fine until about **2034**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to plan properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where families can actually prepare. I'd say people should talk to their parents and children about it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have a good working decade, and the work would end around 2036. That's real, but I'd be 37 with children in school and a house. I could change slowly and carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep interpreting as long as clients want me. I'd help Daniel start his own electrical firm by putting some of our savings into a van and tools, so he's his own boss before the robots. And we'd have our children in the next few years as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious underneath, but steady. It's far away enough to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why invest in Daniel's firm rather than your own future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Daniel's work lasts longer than mine in every picture. If one of us builds something, it should be the one with more time. My part is the books and the customers, which I'm good at from my parents' shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once other interpreters show it's reliable. I'd use it for the reports and to prepare for factory visits. Not instead of me, but next to me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for me alone, but because Daniel's work goes three years later and we'd have a small child. What would help is a way for families to keep small businesses going, like cheaper loans for family shops, and apprenticeships for people changing trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the visitors. When a Japanese buyer comes to a factory far from home, part of my job is making that buyer feel welcome. I don't know if a machine can do that, and I don't think the buyer would want it to.

headlineQuote: When a Japanese buyer comes to a factory far from home, part of my job is making that buyer feel welcome.
portrait: Hana is a 27-year-old **interpreter and translator**, Japanese and English, working factory visits and quality reports.
She's married to Daniel, an **electrician**, and they own a small house with nine months saved.
She uses AI **now and then**, only after seeing it work for others.
She moves from calm to **alarmed** at AGI in two years, then steadies with more time.
Her plans run through **family**: a baby, her parents' shop and Daniel's own firm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Daniel's work follows three years later with a small child.
whatWouldHelp: Cheaper **loans for family shops** and small businesses.
